source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET, quantum physics)
finding: Built a concept co-occurrence network from 750,000 quantum physics papers (since 1919). A neural net trained on past network states predicts which unlinked concept pairs will link later.
numbers: AUC 0.85 for the 2017 test year (0.5 = random). About 5% of edges are drawn in the test year. Evaluation restricted to concept pairs sharing under 20% of neighbours.
limits: Predicts links in a field's own literature. Says nothing about whether a link is worth pursuing.
agent_relevance: Co-occurrence graph memory can rank which concept pairs are likely to be joined; a cheap prior for analogue retrieval, not a validity check.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Predicting the Future of AI with AI (Science4Cast benchmark)
finding: Benchmark: AI concept network with 64,719 concept nodes and about 18 million edges from over 100,000 arXiv papers. Ten methods compared, from pure statistics to pure learning.
numbers: Doubling time of AI papers about 23 months. Single new edge prediction was the competition task; for strong links (formed 3 or more times) AUC beyond 99%.
limits: Edges are co-mentions in title or abstract, not shown to be meaningful. Strong-link prediction is easy because it follows existing hubs.
agent_relevance: High AUC mostly reflects preferential attachment. Do not treat network-predicted links as evidence of insight.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Science4Cast: hand-crafted versus learned features
finding: Models using carefully hand-crafted network features beat methods that learn features end to end. The best entries combined hand-crafted features with machine learning.
numbers: Ten methods, measured by ROC AUC; learned-only models often fell below AUC 0.6 or were too costly to compute on 10 million test pairs.
limits: Competition setting, one domain (AI), one time split (2021).
agent_relevance: Simple graph statistics (common neighbours, degree) are a strong baseline an agent should try before heavy learned retrieval.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Science4Cast: network growth properties
finding: The network grows by hubs. A few concepts take a growing share of new edges. Clustering falls over time.
numbers: Average clustering coefficient by year: 1999 0.919, 2004 0.844, 2009 0.773, 2013 0.650. Degree distribution: truncated power law and lognormal fit better than plain power law (p about 0.003 to 0.015).
limits: Descriptive, one corpus.
agent_relevance: Memory graphs drift toward hubs; retrieval should correct for popularity so rare analogues surface.

source: Gu & Krenn (2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics via ML on evolving knowledge graphs
finding: Knowledge graph with more than 26 million edges. Four model types (fully connected net, transformer, random forest, XGBoost) predict future links and the citations of new concept pairs.
numbers: AUC beyond 0.9 in most experiments, e.g. fcNN 0.963, XGBoost 0.960, Transformer 0.957, Forest 0.953 in the first setting; random 0.5. 141 features per pair, 41 of them network features. Top-predicted pairs got more than 3 orders of magnitude more citations than the average of 10 million pairs.
limits: Impact label is 3-year citation count, a weak proxy for value. Model families end up within about 0.01 AUC of each other.
agent_relevance: Model choice matters little; features matter. Citation-based filters are a poor proxy for usefulness (see SciMuse).

source: Gu & Krenn (2026) SciMuse: interesting scientific ideas from knowledge graphs and LLMs, 100 group leaders
finding: 4,451 personalised ideas built from a 58 million paper graph with an LLM were rated by research group leaders. Ratings were modest. Graph-chosen concept pairs did not beat a titles-only GPT baseline.
numbers: 110 of 267 invited leaders took part (41.2%). Mean interest 2.40 of 5; modal rating 1; 24.9% rated 4 or 5. Means: high-citation-predicted pairs 2.350 +/- 0.034, random pairs 2.446 +/- 0.035, titles-only GPT 2.414 +/- 0.036.
limits: Self-selected responders, mostly natural scientists. Interest is subjective. Order effect small: slope -0.0038 per question, about 0.18 points over 48 questions.
agent_relevance: Key failed result: network structure used for concept-pair selection gave no gain in expert interest. Do not assume graph retrieval improves idea quality.

source: Gu & Krenn (2026) SciMuse: graph features and interest
finding: Predicted citation impact and expert interest pull apart. Graph features still carry some signal for interest, so interest can be predicted.
numbers: High-citation-predicted pairs rated 1.94 in one comparison (weak evidence, lower than random). Semantic distance correlates negatively and Simpson similarity positively with interest; degree Spearman about -0.166. A supervised net on graph features and a zero-shot LLM Elo ranker (22,000 to 45,000 pairwise comparisons) both predicted interest.
limits: Effects are small. Predictors trained on one pool of evaluators.
agent_relevance: Prefer moderately close, well-connected pairs over very distant ones when retrieving analogues; use an LLM pairwise ranker as a cheap filter.

source: Gu & Krenn (2026) SciMuse: participation and selection
finding: Large expert study has selection bias: 58.8% did not take part, mostly non-response.
numbers: 267 invited, 110 participated (41.2%). 138 no reply, 12 lost contact, 6 declined for lack of time, 1 for ethical concerns. Sample mostly natural-science institutes.
limits: Mean rating could differ for non-responders.
agent_relevance: Treat expert-rating results as the view of willing raters.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind review of expert-written ideas versus LLM-agent ideas (retrieval of papers plus over-generate and rerank). LLM ideas were judged more novel.
numbers: 79 reviewers; 49 ideas per condition. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p<0.05), AI plus human rerank 5.81. Review-level table: human n=119 reviews, AI n=109.
limits: Ideas only, no execution. Novelty judged by experts who disagree a lot. Seven NLP topics only.
agent_relevance: LLM ideation with retrieval can look novel to experts; novelty is not the same as correct or feasible.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM ideas: feasibility, excitement, overall
finding: AI ideas scored higher on novelty and excitement but slightly lower on feasibility. Overall score differed only after human reranking.
numbers: Feasibility: human 6.61, AI 6.34, AI+rerank 6.44 (adjusted p=1.00). Excitement: 4.55 vs 5.19 (p=0.04) vs 5.46. Overall: 4.68 vs 4.85 (p=1.00) vs 5.34 (p=0.04).
limits: Multiple-comparison adjusted tests; novelty holds under several corrections but overall score does not without reranking.
agent_relevance: Add a feasibility check after novelty search; novelty gains cost some feasibility.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM ideation lacks diversity
finding: Over-generating ideas saturates quickly: most are duplicates of earlier ones.
numbers: Of 4,000 seed ideas per topic, only about 200 (about 5%) remained after removing pairs with cosine similarity above 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2).
limits: Threshold chosen by manual inspection; one agent design.
agent_relevance: Sampling more candidates from the same memory does not widen the search; need distinct sources or forced distance.

source: Si et al. (2024) Reliability of ideation judgement, human and LLM
finding: Human reviewers of ideas agree only modestly. LLM judges are no better than humans on this task.
numbers: Reviewer agreement 56.1% (random 50%), versus 66.0% in the NeurIPS 2021 consistency study and 71.9% for 1.2K ICLR 2024 LM submissions. Their Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker reached 53.3% on their own data; on the ICLR proxy, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%.
limits: Agreement metric is a balanced top/bottom-25% split, not Krippendorff alpha.
agent_relevance: LLM self-evaluation of ideas is near chance; do not gate on it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Retrieves 'inspirations' (semantic neighbours, knowledge-graph neighbours, citation neighbours) then generates ideas and iteratively compares to prior papers to boost novelty. GPT-4 alone gives low novelty and technical depth.
numbers: GPT4 few-shot beat zero-shot in 65% of preliminary human comparisons. Iterative novelty boosting: first round raised novelty in 54.4% of GPT4FS ideas, 55.6% with semantic neighbours, 47.8% citation, 46.7% KG; second round 57.8% (semantic). New terms +22.8%. Six NLP-expert annotators, 50 instances.
limits: Small human study. Information extraction pipeline: 79.7% of instances pass all steps; relation extraction precision only 65%.
agent_relevance: A novelty check against retrieved prior art works, but retrieval noise in the graph limits it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: inspiration retrieval ablation
finding: GPT4FS and GPT4FS plus knowledge-graph inspirations outperform smaller fine-tuned models by a wide margin; the KG variant tends to give more technical ideas. Generated ideas still fall short of real paper ideas.
numbers: Table 2 vote shares: GPT4FS and GPT4FS+KG far ahead of T5 variants. Exact percentages not transcribed here.
limits: Evaluation by six volunteers.
agent_relevance: Graph neighbours help generation modestly; they do not replace judgement.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware AI
finding: Embedding models that also encode which scientists work on what predict future discoveries far better than content-only models, especially when literature is sparse.
numbers: Up to 400% better precision. Materials: about 100% average gain; drug-disease (CTD) 43% higher precision at 18 years; ClinicalTrials: 36% and 38% of predictions confirmed, rising to 42%, versus 10-12% for content-only (350-400% higher). Gain correlates with drug mention frequency r=0.74, p<0.001.
limits: Retrospective tests; works best for frequently mentioned entities.
agent_relevance: Social structure predicts discovery beyond text. An agent has one mind, so this is mostly a limit.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) predicting the scientists who will discover
finding: The model also predicts who will make a discovery. Removing authors from the graph drops precision.
numbers: Over 17 prediction years (2001 to 2017): 40% of top-50 ranked authors made thermoelectric and ferroelectric discoveries one year later; 20% for photovoltaics. Author-less graph precision 48%, 50%, 58% versus 62%, 58%, 74% for full graph.
limits: Author prediction partly reflects who already publishes on the topic.
agent_relevance: Prediction of the next step rewards the conventional path.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) avoiding the crowd to find alien hypotheses
finding: Tuning the model away from what experts would likely do yields hypotheses that humans take longer to reach, or never reach in the test window.
numbers: Average discovery wait time climbs as the avoidance parameter increases for energy properties, COVID-19 prevention and treatment, and 70% of other diseases. For COVID-19 none of the predictions at parameter above 0.4 were discovered by humans in the window.
limits: No ground truth that unreached hypotheses are correct; unreached may mean wrong.
agent_relevance: A 'distance from the crowd' dial is a tunable operator, but needs a validity test as well.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster & Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery (PNAS)
finding: Typical research strategy in biomedicine is conservative and gets more conservative. Efficient early, inefficient for mature networks. Risk taking and publishing failures would speed discovery.
numbers: Data: 2,363,858 MEDLINE articles and 295,812 patents, 1976 to 2010, 30,060 chemicals, 1,338,753 unique relationships. Most efficient at about 13% of the network discovered. At 50% discovered, relative loss: optimal about 33.6, coordinated 13.4, MEDLINE 95.7, random 271.4 (typical about 2.8 times optimal; text says over three times costlier).
limits: Efficiency counts only novel links; repeat work for reliability is unrewarded. Simulations on a degree-preserving sample; 14% soft false-positive rate in annotation; failed experiments missing from data.
agent_relevance: Pure exploitation of hubs is efficient early and wasteful later; schedule exploration by how mature the memory is.

source: Rzhetsky et al. (2015) distances of new links
finding: Most links join already linked chemicals; most new links join chemicals two steps apart; prize winners bridge disconnected components more often.
numbers: Distance one is the bulk of links; distance two the most common for novel links, then disconnected components; other distances extremely rare.
limits: Chemical co-occurrence in an abstract is only an approximation of a relationship.
agent_relevance: Two-step analogues are the common productive reach; bridging gaps is rarer and linked to top work.

source: Shi & Evans (2023) Surprising combinations of research contents and contexts (Nature Communications)
finding: A hypergraph model tells surprising from expected combinations of content (keywords) and context (cited journals). Surprise predicts hit papers.
numbers: Distinguishes real from random combinations more than 95% of the time in biomedicine, physical sciences and patents. In MEDLINE, most surprising context combos are about 4 times as likely to be top-10% cited, content combos 2 times, both about 5 times. Nearly 50% of papers in the top joint novelty group are hits. Patents: 2 times.
limits: Correlational; citations as impact. Up to 50% of outsized impact predictable from improbability.
agent_relevance: Distant combination plus within-topic content is the pattern; surprise is rewarded but not guaranteed.

source: Shi & Evans (2023) context novelty versus content novelty, Nobel and award papers
finding: Content and context novelty can diverge. Nobel prize papers have high content novelty but lower-than-average context novelty.
numbers: Example: a paper at the 97th percentile of context novelty but 15th of content novelty. Scientists cite contexts similar to their venue about 500% more than distant ones.
limits: Few examples; descriptive.
agent_relevance: Distant sources alone are not the winning move; novelty inside the topic matters for top impact.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature (Nature), via ScienceDaily summary
finding: Word2vec on materials abstracts captures periodic-table structure and recommends thermoelectric materials years before discovery. Read: press summary and Europe PMC abstract, not the full paper.
numbers: 3.3 million abstracts, 1922 to 2018, over 1,000 journals, about 500,000 words, 200 dimensions. Using abstracts up to 2000, predicted materials were studied later about four times more often than random. Three of top five from data to 2008 later found. Top-10 predictions all above average computed power factor.
limits: Press-level numbers; ranking by cosine to 'thermoelectric'. Sourati and Evans report content-only embeddings about half as precise as human-aware ones.
agent_relevance: Embedding similarity to a goal term is a cheap retrieval cue and beat random about four-fold.

source: Cross-study check: network link prediction versus expert-valued ideas
finding: Across Krenn, Gu and Si, structural prediction scores are high (AUC 0.85 to 0.99) but expert-rated idea value is modest or no better than baseline.
numbers: AUC 0.85 (SEMNET), above 0.9 (Gu and Krenn), 99%+ for strong links, versus SciMuse mean 2.40 of 5 and graph pairs not above GPT baseline.
limits: Synthesis by this agent from the opened papers; different tasks and raters.
agent_relevance: Do not use link-prediction accuracy as a quality proxy; test retrieved analogues against real downstream use.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Science4Cast: concentration of edges in hubs
finding: A small fraction of nodes supplies a growing share of new edges; the least connected nodes contribute few.
numbers: Edges from nodes in and below the 80th degree percentile form a shrinking share over 1999 to 2013 (Fig. 5). Network has 64,719 nodes.
limits: Exact share values read from a figure, not transcribed.
agent_relevance: Popularity bias: retrieval by degree returns the famous, not the useful.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) abstract-level claim (Europe PMC record)
finding: Latent knowledge about future discoveries is to a large extent embedded in past publications; no human labelling needed.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports using unsupervised embeddings as a memory index.

source: Rzhetsky et al. (2015) policy claim
finding: Strategy is inefficient for science as a whole; shifts in grants, evaluation and publication of failures are needed.
numbers: Thousands of alternative strategies tested on a network sample by supercomputer.
limits: Policy argument beyond the data; only part of the page was read.
agent_relevance: Keep a log of failed attempts in memory; the paper treats unpublished failure as a loss.
